outcome: No proof or refutation of the Hadamard conjecture has appeared since 26 January 2024. The one event that moved the question is an X announcement dated 12 August 2026 by Levent Alpöge with Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle, crediting Claude, of ±1 matrices for twelve orders below 2000 including order 668, the smallest order with no known Hadamard matrix; it has no paper, is not peer reviewed, and Epoch AI's benchmark lists the order-668 item as a provisional solve, now labelled 'Solved (human + AI)'.
problem_asks: Read from the statement alone: (1) for every positive integer k, i.e. for each of the infinitely many orders n = 4k (4, 8, 12, ...); (2) a Hadamard matrix of order 4k must exist, meaning an n-by-n matrix with entries in {+1, -1} whose rows are mutually orthogonal (H·Hᵀ = n·I). The statement asks for existence only, uniformly over k. It does not ask for a construction, a bound, a count of exceptional orders, or non-existence for any other order. Part (1) and part (2) are one universal claim, so the question is whether that claim holds for all k.

events.what_happened: Sawade is credited with constructing a Hadamard matrix of order 268 in 1985, which made 268 the second-smallest open order before 428. Source: a search-result summary of Eliahou's 2025 AJC note and a search summary citing Graphs and Combinatorics vol. 1 (1985) pp. 185-187. I did not open the Sawade paper or the AJC full text, so this rests on secondary reports.
events.delivers: A Hadamard matrix of order 268, a single instance of the universal claim.
events.remains: All other orders 4k, including the whole universal statement.
events.direction: Confirms an instance; does not touch the universal claim.
events.object: A Hadamard matrix of order 268. Construction method not established in my sources.

events.what_happened: A 32-modular Hadamard matrix of order 668 was known from 2001, per the abstract of Eliahou's AJC note ('A 32-modular Hadamard matrix of that order has been known since 2001'). Author and venue of the 2001 result were not identified in my sources.
events.delivers: A ±1 square matrix H of order 668 with H·Hᵀ ≡ 668·I (mod 32). This is a modular relaxation, not an integer Hadamard matrix.
events.remains: An integer Hadamard matrix of order 668, and the universal claim.
events.direction: Partial modular progress on order 668; cuts neither way on integer existence.
events.object: A 32-modular ±1 matrix of order 668, explicit in the sense that its existence is stated; construction not read.

events.what_happened: Kharaghani and Tayfeh-Rezaie found a Hadamard matrix of order 428. The IPM bulletin announcement is dated 21 June 2004 per a search-result snippet; the published paper 'A Hadamard matrix of order 428' appeared in J. Combin. Designs 13 (2005) 435-440 per search results. Sources disagree on the year (2004 announcement vs 2005 publication). The 428 matrix was the smallest open order until 2005 per secondary reports.
events.revisions: Announcement 2004 (IPM bulletin); journal version 2005 (J. Combin. Designs 13).
events.delivers: A Hadamard matrix of order 428, a single instance of the universal claim. Turyn-type sequences of lengths 36, 36, 36, 35 found by computer search, per the paper's abstract as summarised in a search result.
events.remains: All other orders 4k, including the universal statement.
events.direction: Confirms an instance; does not touch the universal claim.
events.object: A Hadamard matrix of order 428 found by computer search over Turyn-type sequences of lengths 36, 36, 36, 35 (per search-result summary of the abstract).

events.what_happened: Đoković posted 'Hadamard matrices of order 764 exist' on arXiv (math/0703312), constructing two Hadamard matrices of order 764 by the Goethals-Seidel method. Published as Combinatorica 28(4) (2008) 487-489 per search results.
events.delivers: Two Hadamard matrices of order 764, single instances of the universal claim.
events.remains: All other orders 4k, including the universal statement.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal publication of the paper (publication recorded in search results; refereeing not examined)

events.directly_checkable: The two matrices of order 764 are explicit Goethals-Seidel arrays built over Z_191; checkable by computing H·Hᵀ, not done by me.
events.direction: Confirms an instance; does not touch the universal claim.
events.object: Two Hadamard matrices of order 764 of Goethals-Seidel type, explicit (built from a cyclic construction over the prime 191 per the paper's note as summarised in search results).

events.what_happened: Đoković, Golubitsky and Kotsireas constructed Hadamard matrices of orders 1004 (=4·251) and 2524 (=4·631) via Goethals-Seidel arrays and cyclic supplementary difference sets, arXiv 1301.3671 (v1 January 2013 by arXiv number; v2 14 May 2013). I read the arXiv listing only via a search snippet and did not open the paper.
events.delivers: Hadamard matrices of orders 1004 and 2524, single instances of the universal claim.
events.remains: All other orders 4k, including the universal statement.
events.direction: Confirms instances; does not touch the universal claim.
events.object: Hadamard matrices of orders 1004 and 2524 from Goethals-Seidel arrays on cyclic supplementary difference sets (per search-result summary of the paper; not verified by me).

events.what_happened: Shalom Eliahou, 'A 64-modular Hadamard matrix of order 668', Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 93(2) (2025) pp. 422-427, received 24 September 2025 (per the AJC page). It constructs a ±1 matrix H of order 668 with H·Hᵀ ≡ 668·I (mod 64). The abstract states: 'Since 2005, the smallest open case in Hadamard's conjecture from 1893 is n=668.'
events.delivers: A 64-modular (mod 64) ±1 matrix of order 668 with H·Hᵀ ≡ 668·I (mod 64). This is a congruence condition, not an integer Hadamard matrix. Restricted to order 668.
events.remains: An integer Hadamard matrix of order 668, and the universal claim for all k.
events.directly_checkable: The mod-64 identity H·Hᵀ ≡ 668·I can be checked on the matrix, which is given in the paper (not read by me; the PDF was not readable here).
events.direction: Partial progress: a modular relaxation at 668. It does not give the object the conjecture asserts and so cuts neither way on the existence of an integer Hadamard matrix of order 668.
events.object: A square ±1 matrix H of order 668 with H·Hᵀ ≡ 668·I (mod 64). Explicit as far as I can tell; construction not read.

events.what_happened: Ramos, Hulak and de Queiroz, 'Multiplier obstructions for Legendre pairs of length 333', arXiv 2607.20765, submitted 22 July 2026. A Legendre pair of length 333 would yield a Hadamard matrix of order 668. The paper shows that under a common-multiplier symmetry condition such pairs can exist only if the subgroup has order at most 6, and rules out 21 of the 30 candidate subgroups.
events.delivers: An obstruction to one route to order 668: symmetric Legendre pairs of length 333 with a common multiplier subgroup of order at least 9 are excluded for 19 subgroups, and 21 of 30 candidate subgroups are excluded in all. Restricted to the fixed-multiplier case.
events.remains: Unrestricted existence of a Legendre pair of length 333, which would give order 668 by this route; the order-668 Hadamard question; and the universal claim. The abstract says 'the unrestricted existence problems remain open'.
events.direction: Obstruction within one construction route; produces no object; cuts neither way on existence at 668.
people: Ruy J. G. B. de Queiroz

events.what_happened: On 12 August 2026 Levent Alpöge, with Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle and Claude, announced on X ±1 matrices for twelve orders below 2000 that had no known Hadamard matrix: 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948, 1964. No paper was posted. The announcement was a block of 23,828 '+' and '-' signs, with an obfuscated shell-script decoder in the replies. The original X post could not be read here (HTTP 402); its content is known from secondary reports (QbitAI, Pedaily, BAAI, Aliteq), a blog quoting the post (Ion Nechita, 13 Aug 2026), a John D. Cook blog post (13 Aug 2026), Epoch AI's problem page and changelog, and a Wikipedia summary. Epoch's changelog dates its entry 2026-08-12. The matrices were reproduced by a database called VibeMathed (per QbitAI/BAAI reports) and by others; I did not run the decoder.
events.revisions: No revised text, paper or technical report found through the latest dated source I found (24 September 2026). Epoch's classification of the order-668 item was changed after the first entry (see checked_by and disputes); the announcement itself was not revised.
events.delivers: Reported explicit ±1 matrices, one for each of twelve orders below 2000 (668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948, 1964), each reported to satisfy H·Hᵀ = n·I exactly. For 668 the reproducers report diagonal entries 668 and maximum off-diagonal absolute value 0. Restrictions: finitely many orders, all below 2000; no general construction, infinite family, or method is published; each order is one instance of the universal claim. The claim that these are all admissible orders below 2000 that were open matches the 12-order list in Wikipedia's Hadamard article (citing Đoković, Golubitsky and Kotsireas, 2014) and a March 2024 ProofWiki list, but I did not verify that census independently.
events.remains: The universal statement: a Hadamard matrix of order 4k for every positive integer k. Also open: every order 4k at or above 2000 (none of the sources I opened says whether any such order is currently known); the method, so whether the twelve orders reflect a general construction; and any order below 2000 outside the 2014/2024 lists.

checked_by.who: Epoch AI (FrontierMath: Open Problems), the benchmark organiser
checked_by.qualification: Runs the benchmark and its per-problem verifiers; not an independent mathematical referee
checked_by.what_they_did: Changelog 2026-08-12 marked the order-668 item 'solved by AI', provisionally, on a report from an Anthropic researcher crediting 'a team of three humans and Claude'. The page later reads 'Solved (human + AI)' with 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)'; a 2026-09-16 changelog entry (per a summary of the Epoch listing) introduced the 'human + AI' label. Epoch's FAQ says a verifier-accepted AI solution is recorded on the problem page, and that a solution 'confirmed by a mathematician' increments the headline chart; I found no record of a mathematician confirmation for this item.

checked_by.who: Ion Nechita (blogger; professional standing not established in my sources)
checked_by.qualification: Author of the blog post, which reports his own check
checked_by.what_they_did: Reports saving the tweet text, having Codex write a short Python script to check that entries are ±1 and H·Hᵀ = n·I, and reports the check passed. The check itself was machine-run; the human part is setting it up and reporting it. The same post gives his own unverified guess at the method ('a very strong model', compute, an agentic harness), which is speculation, not the authors' account.

checked_by.who: VibeMathed (described in QbitAI/BAAI reports as an independent database of mathematical results)
checked_by.qualification: Could not be identified in my searches; no URL found
checked_by.what_they_did: Reportedly reproduced the decoding into twelve sign patterns and checked them with exact integer arithmetic (entries ±1, zero pairwise row inner products; for 668, diagonal 668 and maximum off-diagonal 0). Reported only through secondary coverage.

events.time_since_posted: since 12 August 2026; the latest dated item I found is 24 September 2026, about six weeks later. No mathematician's written assessment of the method or of the claimed census was found.

machine_checked.system: Exact-integer check of H·Hᵀ = n·I by reproducers (reported, not inspected). Epoch's custom verifier: inferred, not seen. Epoch's FAQ says a verifier-accepted AI solution gets its status recorded; the solved label implies the verifier accepted the 668 matrix, but I did not inspect the verifier.

events.directly_checkable: Yes in principle. Run the decoder shell script posted in the replies to the 12 August post on the 23,828-sign string, then check H·Hᵀ = n·I in exact integer arithmetic for each output. The reported 668 result is a diagonal of 668 and off-diagonal zeros. I did not retrieve the post or run the decoder.
events.doubts: (a) No paper, technical report or written proof; the only public artefact described is a sign string plus a decoder in the replies, reported via secondary coverage. The Chinese-language report says it cannot yet be told whether this is an improved search or a general construction (QbitAI/BAAI, via summarising fetch). (b) The original post could not be read by me; every detail of the decoder, counts and checks comes from secondary reports, and Aliteq publishes near-duplicate pages with different bylines. (c) Epoch's own label moved from 'solved by AI' (provisional, 12 Aug) to 'Solved (human + AI)', which Epoch says it would revise if team reports show humans contributed significantly to the core ideas; the AI attribution is therefore contested by the benchmark's own record. (d) Status snapshots conflict: TheoremDB (reviewed 24 July 2026, before the announcement) lists 668 as open; an undated GitHub gist says the construction 'does not resolve the existence of a Hadamard matrix of order 668'; ProofWatch tags a GitHub 'H.668 verified' note and a mathdb entry as rumours. (e) Kulhandjian's 22 September 2026 arXiv abstract calls 668 'the smallest open Hadamard order' and does not mention the August claim (abstract read only). (f) The 12-order completeness claim depends on the 2014/2024 census, which I did not check. I found no specific error identified in any key step, and no withdrawal or retraction.
events.direction: Cuts in favour of the conjecture for each listed order: each is a claimed existence of an order that the conjecture predicts, and no source reports any order 4k lacking a Hadamard matrix. As instances of a universal claim, these confirm cases; they do not contradict the statement. The reported 12 orders also remove the entries from the list of open orders below 2000.
events.object: Explicit as reported: a block of 23,828 '+' and '-' signs posted on X, with a shell-script decoder in the replies, decodes to twelve ±1 matrices of orders 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948 and 1964. For the order-668 matrix, reproducers report H·Hᵀ = 668·I exactly (diagonal 668, maximum off-diagonal absolute value 0). The generating method is not published; I did not retrieve the matrices.
people: Levent Alpöge (credited as an Anthropic researcher by Epoch and secondary reports)

systems.name: Claude (internal Anthropic model)
systems.what_it_did: The authors do not say what Claude did. Epoch's problem page credits the solution to 'a team of three humans and Claude' and records 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)'. The only own-account statement I found is a casual credit in the post as quoted by Nechita, listing collaborators. Whether Claude contributed the idea, the construction, or only checking or coding is not established. The Chinese-language reports say how Claude contributed awaits a technical report.
systems.basis_quote: weekend fun w @tehwalris, Saul Reynolds-Haertle, and of course claude:))

events.what_happened: Manuel González-Regadera and Raúl M. Falcón, 'A computational framework for multidimensional loop-cocyclic Hadamard matrices', arXiv 2609.18380, submitted 16 September 2026. It extends the cocyclic development of Hadamard matrices to finite loops and reports computations for groups of orders 4 and 8 and one non-associative loop of order 8. It does not concern the order-668 existence question as stated in its abstract.
events.delivers: A computational framework and classification results for loop-cocyclic Hadamard matrices of small orders. Nothing at order 668.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks is untouched by this paper.
events.doubts: A secondary search summary says its bibliography cites the 12 August announcement as an 'electronic announcement and source code repository' with 'Claude-Anthropic' as an author. I could not read the reference list (PDF not readable here), so this link is unverified and the paper is not evidence for or against the 668 claim.
events.direction: Does not bear on the universal claim or on order 668.

events.what_happened: Michel Kulhandjian, 'An explicit half-flip family of 32-modular Hadamard matrices at L = 3 mod 8', arXiv 2609.25543, submitted 22 September 2026. The abstract is motivated by Eliahou's 64-modular construction 'at the smallest open Hadamard order n=668' and gives a family of 32-modular matrices. It does not mention the August announcement in the abstract (abstract read only; full text not read).
events.delivers: An explicit family of 32-modular Hadamard matrices at L ≡ 3 mod 8. Modular (mod 32), not integer Hadamard matrices. No new integer Hadamard matrix at 668 is claimed.
events.remains: An integer Hadamard matrix of order 668, and the universal claim.
events.doubts: Later-work signal: the abstract still calls 668 'the smallest open Hadamard order' and cites Eliahou's modular note, without mentioning the 12 August claim. This rests on the abstract only.
events.direction: Modular progress at 668; cuts neither way on integer existence.
events.object: A family of 32-modular ±1 matrices at L ≡ 3 mod 8, explicit per the abstract; construction not read.

events.what_happened: Williamson, Yacobi and Zinn-Justin, 'Generating Hadamard matrices with transformers', arXiv 2604.11101, submitted 13 April 2026 (last revised 11 May 2026). Transformer neural networks with local search in the PatternBoost framework construct Hadamard matrices, with the largest example of order 252 per the arXiv abstract (a catalogue mirror gives 244, a version difference). Orders are at most 252, all already known, and the paper does not claim a new order at or above 668.
events.delivers: Many inequivalent Hadamard matrices of orders roughly 100 to 252, by a learned-model-plus-search method. No order in the problem's open set is reached.
events.remains: The universal claim and every order at or above 668 that is open.
events.directly_checkable: The matrices are checkable by H·Hᵀ = n·I; not checked by me.
events.doubts: The arXiv abstract's largest order (252) and a catalogue mirror's (244) differ; I did not open the paper's full text to resolve it.
events.direction: Does not bear on the universal claim or on any open order; it is an AI-involved method for orders already known.
events.object: Hadamard matrices of orders up to 252 (largest 252 per abstract), of Goethals-Seidel type found by the method. None at an open order.

systems.name: transformer neural networks with local search in the PatternBoost framework
systems.what_it_did: Generated Hadamard matrices of orders up to 252 (as stated in the abstract); this is a method built around transformer models, not a named lab model. Its contribution is load-bearing for those matrices but not for any open order.
systems.basis_quote: We present a new method for constructing Hadamard matrices that combines transformer neural networks with local search in the PatternBoost framework.

disputes.summary: Whether AI solved the order-668 item is contested within the record. Epoch's changelog marked it 'solved by AI' on 2026-08-12 (provisional). The current problem page reads 'Solved (human + AI)' with 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)'. Chinese-language and Aliteq reports say AI solved it; the announcing blogger writes 'humans have found a Hadamard matrix of order 668'; the authors' only statement found is 'and of course claude:))' within a collaborator list. Epoch says it will revise if humans contributed significantly to the core ideas. I did not decide which reading holds.

Conflicting status reports on order 668. TheoremDB (reviewed 24 July 2026, before the announcement) lists it as open with a note that live status could not be refreshed; an undated GitHub gist says the construction does not resolve existence; ProofWatch tags a GitHub 'verified' note and a mathdb entry as rumours; a Hacker News thread of 15 September 2026 is titled 'Hadamard matrix of order 668 Solved?' (not opened). The July arXiv paper 2607.20765 says 668 'remains unresolved' and predates the claim.

Date of the 428 result: the IPM announcement is dated 2004 (search snippet, page not opened because of a certificate error) while the published paper is J. Combin. Designs 2005. Only the year matters for the 2026 question, and this is a pre-window event.

summary: Nothing has been proved about the universal Hadamard conjecture since 26 January 2024, and nothing in the record refutes it. The event that matters is the 12 August 2026 X announcement by Levent Alpöge with Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle, crediting Claude, of ±1 matrices for twelve orders below 2000 including 668, the smallest order without a known Hadamard matrix. The announcement was a 23,828-sign string with a shell-script decoder in the replies; no paper or technical report has been posted in what I could find. I could not read the original post (HTTP 402), so its content comes from secondary reports (QbitAI, Pedaily, BAAI, Aliteq), a blog that quotes it (Nechita), a John D. Cook post, Epoch AI's problem page and changelog, and a Wikipedia summary. I opened all of those, but several only through a summarising fetch, so quoted wording is paraphrase-prone and should be checked against the originals. Epoch's FrontierMath page (problem added 24 February 2026) marked the item 'solved by AI' provisionally on 12 August 2026 and now reads 'Solved (human + AI)' with 'First solved with: Claude (internal Anthropic model)'. Its credit line 'a team of three humans and Claude' comes from a report by an Anthropic researcher. The authors' only own-account statement I found is the casual 'and of course claude:))' in a collaborator list; no source says what Claude did, and Nechita's method guess is speculation. Reproduction is reported: exact-integer checks by 'VibeMathed' and others give H·Hᵀ with diagonal 668 and zero off-diagonal for the 668 matrix. I could not find VibeMathed and did not run the decoder. Scope: the statement is universal over k, so these twelve finitely many instances confirm cases and move no quantity the statement names; the 12 orders also match the 2014 and March 2024 lists of unknown orders below 2000 (I did not verify those lists independently). Earlier milestones, all before the window, are 268 (Sawade, 1985, secondary), 428 (Kharaghani and Tayfeh-Rezaie, 2004 announcement, 2005 paper), 764 (Đoković, arXiv March 2007), 1004 and 2524 (Đoković, Golubitsky and Kotsireas, 2013), and a 32-modular matrix of order 668 from 2001 whose author and venue I did not identify. Eliahou's 64-modular 668 note (AJC 93(2), 2025; received 24 September 2025) is the best earlier partial result at 668 and is modular, not integer. Later items: Ramos, Hulak and de Queiroz (22 July 2026) give an obstruction to a Legendre-pair route to 668; González-Regadera and Falcón (16 September 2026) are unrelated in their abstract and their reported citation of the announcement is unverified; Kulhandjian (22 September 2026) calls 668 'the smallest open Hadamard order' in its abstract and does not mention the August claim. AI attempts before the announcement did not solve 668: per Epoch, GPT-5.2 Pro solved the 428 warm-up but not 668, and Gemini 3 Deep Think did not solve 668; per a tweet snippet by Motwani (not opened), GPT 5.6 Sol Max Reasoning and Claude Fable were tested on 668 within HorizonMath without success. The Williamson, Yacobi and Zinn-Justin transformer paper (April 2026) is AI-involved but reaches orders of at most 252, all already known. The AI search also turned up AlphaEvolve-style determinant tasks on 29×29 ±1 matrices, which are not Hadamard constructions. Context for the judging pass, not researched: the same author has announced other claims in 2026 (a Jacobian counterexample in July, Carathéodory and Navier–Stokes in August, Hopf's problem on 23 August), per a Wikipedia summary.
competing_reading: Read as an AI success: Epoch lists the 668 item as a benchmark solve credited to Claude, its verifier-based policy records AI solves only when a verifier accepts them, and the team reports the twelve orders below 2000 are all filled. Read as a human-led result with AI as tool: Epoch's current label is 'human + AI', the authors' only own-account statement is a casual credit inside a collaborator list, and the announcement is a sign string with a decoder whose method is unpublished, so the load-bearing contribution of Claude cannot be read from the record. On scope, a reader who treats the statement as only about order 668 (Epoch's framing) would count one solved item; a reader who holds the statement to its universal form would count zero moved, since twelve instances do not move a universal claim.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The 12 August post's decoder and the twelve matrices, checked by someone other than the reproducers already reported; (2) the promised technical report or a paper stating how the matrices were found and what Claude contributed; (3) Epoch's written rationale for the 2026-09-16 'human + AI' relabel and whether a mathematician confirmed the solution under its FAQ; (4) an independent census of admissible orders below 2000 showing exactly which twelve were open before 12 August 2026; (5) for the universal claim, nothing short of a general construction or a new family would move the statement.

events.ai_basis: We present a new method for constructing Hadamard matrices that combines transformer neural networks with local search in the PatternBoost framework.
ai_systems_credited: transformer neural networks with local search in the PatternBoost framework

judgement.why: The statement is universal over all k, so every construction of a Hadamard matrix at specific orders — Sawade, Kharaghani–Tayfeh-Rezaie, Đoković, DGK, the transformer paper, and the 12 August 2026 twelve-order announcement — is a finite set of instances (F5), however notable 668 is as the smallest open order; the 'smallest unknown order' is not a quantity the statement names, so I did not read the announcement as a bound. Modular (mod 32/64) matrices change the question (variant); the Legendre-pair obstruction and the loop-cocyclic framework settle nothing (none). Direction is null for all since none is a case/whole. For the Alpöge announcement the only own-account AI statement is 'weekend fun w @tehwalris, Saul Reynolds-Haertle, and of course claude:))', which does not say Claude produced any mathematics, so ai_role none; Epoch's 'first solved with Claude' label is the benchmark's attribution, not the authors' account. The transformer paper's quote does say the learned model generates the matrices (generated), but it reaches only known orders. Đoković 764 counted digested via Combinatorica; Eliahou via AJC publication.
judgement.doubts: If one reads the 'smallest open order' frontier as a bound on the problem, the August 2026 announcement would be a bound with an unclear AI role; I rejected that reading per the statement's universal wording. The AI contribution to the announcement is unknown pending a technical report; Epoch credits Claude but the authors have not said what it did.
